'''Robin Jon Hawes Clark''' {{post-nominals|country=NZL|CNZM|FRS}} (16 February 1935 – 6 December 2018) was a New Zealand-born chemist initially noted for research of [[Coordination complex|transition metal]] and [[mixed-valence]] complexes, and later for the use of [[Raman spectroscopy]] in determining the chemical composition of pigments used in artworks.

==Early life and education==
Clark was born in [[Rangiora, New Zealand]] on 16 February 1935, to parents Reginald Hawes Clark and Marjorie Alice Clark. He attended [[Marlborough College, Blenheim]], and [[Christ's College, Christchurch]] before pursuing bachelor's and master's at [[University of Canterbury|Canterbury University College]]. Clark was a research and teaching fellow under [[William Fyfe (geochemist)|William Fyfe]] at the [[University of Otago]] in 1958. From 1958 to 1961, Clark worked toward a doctorate advised by [[Ronald Sydney Nyholm]] and [[Jack Lewis, Baron Lewis of Newnham|Jack Lewis]] at [[University College London]] and was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree for his work on titanium complexes in 1961. The [[University of London]] later awarded Clark a [[Doctor of Science#United Kingdom, Ireland, India, Pakistan and the Commonwealth|DSc]] in 1969.<ref name="aecv">{{cite news |title=Professor Robin J H Clark CNZM FRS |url=https://www.ae-info.org/attach/User/Clark_Robin/CV/CV_Clark.pdf |access-date=15 December 2018 |publisher=Academia Europaea}}</ref><ref name="ww">{{cite journal |title=Clark, Prof. Robin Jon Hawes |journal=Who's Who in the United Kingdom |date=2010 |doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U11033}}</ref>

==Career==
Clark began teaching at [[University College London]] in 1962 as an assistant lecturer. He was appointed [[Sir William Ramsay]] Professor in 1989, and served until retirement in 2009. He served as the dean of science from 1988 to 1989 and later as head of the chemistry department from 1989 to 1999.

Clark died in London on 6 December 2018.<ref>{{cite news |title=Robin Clark: Biography |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/robin-clark-11228/ |access-date=15 December 2018 |publisher=The Royal Society}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Prof. Robin Clark |url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/thetimes-uk/obituary.aspx?pid=190971946 |access-date=15 December 2018 |work=The Times |date=12 December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=http://deaths.marlexpress.co.nz/obituaries/marlborough-express-nz/obituary.aspx?n=robin-clark&pid=191010421 | title=Robin Clark death notice | date=16 December 2018 | work=Marlborough Express | access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref>

===Artwork authentication===
In 1992, Clark was asked to develop a non-destructive technique to analyze the chemical composition of a painting in such a way to be able to spot art forgeries. He had since developed the use of [[Raman spectroscopy]] as an important tool for use in the fields of artwork authentication, conservation, and preservation.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i51/Robin-Clark.html |title=Robin Clark: Chemist describes the challenges of authenticating artwork and finding forgeries |journal=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |date=17 December 2012 |volume=90 |issue=51 |page=36 |first=Sarah |last=Everts|doi=10.1021/cen-09051-scitech3 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1039/cs9952400187 |title=Raman Microscopy: Application to the Identification of Pigments on Medieval Manuscripts |journal=[[Chemical Society Reviews]] |year=1995 |volume=24 |pages=187–196 |first=Robin J. H. |last=Clark|issue=3 }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Over the course of his career, Clark delivered several named lectures and received multiple awards. In 1969, he was elected a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]. In 1989, he was granted honorary fellowship by the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]]. He became a fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Davies|first1=Alwyn G.|last2=McMillan|first2=Paul F.|date=2020|title=Robin Jon Hawes Clark. 16 February 1935—6 December 2018|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=68|pages=103–129|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2019.0037|s2cid=210039438|doi-access=free}}</ref> and member of the [[Academia Europaea]] in 1990. Two years later, he was elected a fellow of University College London and the [[Royal Society of Arts]], and in 2001 he was conferred with an honorary DSc by the [[University of Canterbury]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Honorary graduates |url= https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/media/images/leadership-and-governance/Honorary_Graduates_Annual_Recipient_List.pdf |publisher=University of Canterbury |access-date=17 December 2018 |page=2 }}</ref> Clark was appointed a [[Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit]] in the [[2004 Birthday Honours (New Zealand)|2004 Queen's Birthday Honours]], for services to science and New Zealand interests in the United Kingdom,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://dpmc.govt.nz/publications/queens-birthday-honours-list-2004 |title=Queen's Birthday honours list 2004 |date=7 June 2004 |publisher=Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet |access-date=17 December 2018}}</ref> followed by elections as a foreign fellow of the [[National Academy of Sciences, India]] in 2007 and as an international member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2010.<ref name="aecv"/> In 2009, Royal Society of Chemistry awarded Clark the [[Sir George Stokes Award]] for his contribution to the application of analytical science to the arts and archaeology through his development of Raman microscopy for the identification of pigments.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/SirGeorgeStokesAward/2009winner.asp |title=Sir George Stokes Award 2009 winner |work=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |access-date=24 December 2018}}</ref>
